title: Blood Culture Workflow

references.label: CLSI Standards for Clinical Laboratory Practice

purpose: To detect bloodstream infection (bacteremia/fungemia) by culturing blood in enrichment broth under conditions that favor recovery of even low numbers of circulating organisms.
principle: Blood is normally sterile, so any growth is potentially significant, but skin flora contamination during draw is common — the workflow is built around maximizing sensitivity for true bloodstream infection while giving the laboratory tools (timing, number of bottles, growth pattern) to help distinguish a true positive from a contaminant.
requiredMaterials: Paired aerobic and anaerobic blood culture bottles
requiredReagents: Skin antiseptic for the draw site (e.g. per the laboratory's approved antisepsis protocol)

procedure.instruction: Disinfect the venipuncture site thoroughly per the laboratory's antisepsis protocol to minimize skin-flora contamination — this step is the single largest lever on the contamination rate.

procedure.note: Recommended draw volume is bottle-system-specific; follow the manufacturer's stated volume rather than a generic figure.
procedure.instruction: Draw the volume of blood recommended for the specific bottle system in use, inoculating aerobic and anaerobic bottles as ordered; under-filling reduces sensitivity, over-filling can also affect recovery.
Load bottles promptly into a continuous-monitoring blood culture instrument, which tracks a growth-detection signal (commonly CO2 production) over time.

procedure.note: The rapid preliminary Gram result is one of blood culture's highest-value outputs — it can guide empiric therapy hours before full ID/AST is available.
procedure.instruction: When the instrument flags a bottle positive, perform a Gram stain directly from the bottle and report the preliminary Gram stain/morphology result immediately, ahead of full identification.
Subculture the positive bottle to appropriate solid media for isolation, identification, and susceptibility testing.
If no growth is flagged by the instrument within the validated incubation period for that system, report as no growth to date/final negative per the laboratory's protocol.

observations: Note time-to-positivity, number of bottles/sets positive, and organism(s) recovered relative to what grew in each bottle/set.
interpretation: A single bottle growing a common skin organism (e.g. coagulase-negative Staphylococcus) is often a contaminant, especially if only one of multiple sets/bottles is positive; growth in multiple independently drawn sets, a recognized bloodstream pathogen, or a clinically compatible picture increases the likelihood of true bacteremia — this judgment uses the related contamination-vs-true-isolate concept and is made in correlation with the clinical picture, not from the laboratory result alone.
precautions: Maintain strict skin antisepsis technique to minimize false-positive contamination.
Handle positive bottles as containing viable, potentially pathogenic organisms under appropriate biosafety practice.
limitations: Prior antibiotic therapy can suppress growth and cause a false-negative culture.
Fastidious or slow-growing organisms may require extended incubation or specialized media beyond the standard system.
biosafetyNotes: Positive bottle subculture and Gram stain preparation should be performed using aseptic technique and, depending on suspected organism, within a biosafety cabinet.
